title: HMG Sequencing Workshop
text:
Intended Learning Outcomes
By the end of this practical, you should be able to:

navigate aligned short-read sequencing data in IGV
interpret genes, exons, introns, reading frames, repeats and regulatory annotations
identify candidate sequence variants and distinguish them from likely sequencing or alignment artefacts
assess Mendelian inheritance in a parent-child trio
phase nearby variants into haplotypes using family information and paired reads
investigate population frequency and predicted functional consequences using Ensembl, VEP and gnomAD


Introduction and learning objectives
The advent of next generation sequencing technologies, allowing high-throughput DNA sequencing at relatively low cost, has revolutionised genetics over the last fifteen years or so. In particular the ability to sequence whole human exomes, genomes and transcriptomes, has transformed how we conduct human genetics, yielding radical new approaches to human disease gene identification and allowing us to ask questions largely unimaginable just a few years ago. However, although in many areas it is relatively straightforward to generate DNA sequence data, interpreting the masses of data generated remains a major logistical and bioinformatic challenge. Fortunately, data analysis and interpretation are still largely based on fundamental genetic principles and our knowledge of the molecular pathway from DNA to RNA to protein.
In this session we will familiarise ourselves with a web app version of the Integrated Genome Viewer (IGV). This app allows us to visualise aligned NGS data, to identify sequence variants and to sort neighbouring variants into haplotypes. To do this we will use publicly accessible whole genome sequence data from a parent-child trio derived from the ‘Platinum genomes’, described in:

Eberle, M.A., Fritzilas, E., Krusche, P., Kallberg, M., Moore, B.L., Bekritsky, M.A., Iqbal, Z., Chuang, H.Y., Humphray, S.J., Halpern, A.L., Kruglyak, S., Margulies, E.H., McVean, G. and Bentley, D.R. (2017) A reference data set of 5.4 million phased human variants validated by genetic inheritance from sequencing a three-generation 17-member pedigree. Genome Res. 27, 157-164. https://doi.org/10.1101/gr.210500.116

These short-read data were obtained using whole genome sequencing via paired-end 2x100 bp reads on an Illumina HiSeq2000 platform. Sequencing was performed to an average depth of 50x.

title: 2: Set up IGV and annotation tracks
text:
Use your favourite internet browser to navigate to https://smb-informatics.mvls.gla.ac.uk/igv
(Note: if off campus, you will need to connect using the University VPN - https://www.gla.ac.uk/myglasgow/it/vpn/)
You should see a window like this:

The platinum WGS data we will be using have been aligned to version hg19 of the human reference genome, so we will need to first select the GRCh37/hg19 reference sequence from the genome menu:

In order to interpret the sequence data, we are going to add some additional “Annotation” “Tracks” to the IGV window:

Use Shift+Click to select the Repeat Masker and CpG Islands annotation tracks (in addition to the Refs Genes track which is a default track):

We can also add some known “variants” as a track from the dbSNP database (version 150):

Your window should now look something like this (you can use the grey handle on the right to drag the Refseq Gene annotation back to the top):
crumbs: 2  2: Set up IGV and annotation tracks

title: 3: Navigate the genome
text:
Before looking at any sequence data, get a feel for navigating around the genome and remind yourself of some features of genome organisation.
To see more detail, we need to focus on a smaller region of the genome. There are various ways to do this, including selecting a chromosome either using the pull-down menu, or the chromosome buttons:

Let’s look at chromosome 8:

At this level we can start to see some detail regarding the distribution of known genes (A) and CpG islands (B).

We can zoom in further by either clicking and dragging on the scale (A), typing in sequence coordinates (B), or using the zoom buttons (C).

Try pressing the + zoom button five times:
You should now start to see individual genes and CpG islands. Note how genes and intergenic regions differ in size.

You can press the “Cursor Guide” and “Center Line” buttons to help with navigation.

title: 4: Interpret gene structure using TERF1
text:
Add promoter-associated chromatin data
Once you have zoomed in a bit, you can now also navigate left and right by clicking and dragging the cursor in the data window. Move the TERF1 gene to the centre of the frame:
Exons are indicated by the dark blue boxes with coding regions taller than the non-coding parts of the exons. Introns are indicated by the thin blue line, with the direction of transcription indicated by small arrows (>).
Zoom in to see the structure of the TERF1 gene (there are two primary transcripts for this gene):
Move exon 1 of TERF1 to the centre and zoom in some more. You should start to see the reference sequence appearing. You can also press the cog on the track to turn on “Three-frame translation” to aid in interpretation. This shows the amino acid sequences corresponding to the three possible reading frames of the DNA sequence.
We can add some additional information about the accessibility of DNA in this region by adding an ENCODE Signal track containing ChIP-seq data for H3K4me3 (trimethylation of lysine 4 on histone H3). This histone variant is associated with open chromatin and marks active promoters in the genome, typically appearing near transcription start sites (TSSs).
Add the ENCODE H3K4me3 track and select the ‘GM12878 H3K4me3 | Raw Signal | Biorep 1’ experiment near the bottom of the list and press OK to add the track.
crumbs: 4  4: Interpret gene structure using *TERF1*

title: 4: Interpret gene structure using TERF1
text:
TipTest your understanding




Is CpG island 67 positioned where you expect it to? (zooming in might help)
Why?
Which of the three reading frames do you think is correct for exon 1?
What is the name of the first repeated element in intron 1?









TipAnswer






Yes, CpG island 67 spans a promoter region in exon 1 and associates with H3K4me3 ChIP-seq data (typically found at TSSs and in open chromatin.)
The correct frame starts with an ATG and has no STOP codons within exon 1. It will depend on your particular instance of IGV.
The first repeated element is a MIRb element and there are some additional Alu, LINE and MIR elements, and simple sequence repeats, further down. Note that ~80% of intron 1 sequence is some sort of repeat.
crumbs: 4  4: Interpret gene structure using *TERF1*

title: 4: Interpret gene structure using TERF1
text:
Examine splice junctions
Splice junctions mark the boundaries between exons and introns and are critical for the accurate removal of intronic sequence during RNA splicing. Adjust the view to examine the end of the first exon.






Warning



Be careful - the vertical order of the reading frames sometimes jumps about as you zoom in and out









TipTest your understanding




What is the sequence of the last codon of exon 1?
What is the sequence of the first two bases of the intron?
Why is this important?









TipAnswer






It will depend on your IGV instance but in this image it is the bottom frame as this matches the start codon at the beginning of the transcript, so the last codon is G–
The first two bases of the intron are GT
This is the consensus splice donor site




Adjust the view to examine the end of the first intron and the beginning of the second exon.







TipTest your understanding




What is the sequence of the first codon of exon 2?
What codon is formed after splicing when the final base of exon 1 is combined with the first two bases of exon 2?
Which amino acid does it encode (see below for the genetic code)?
What is the sequence of the last two bases of the intron?
Why is this important?










TipAnswer






The codon so far contains G– and was split by the intron. To make it a complete triplet, the rest of the codon must be the -AT from exon 2.
GAT.
Aspartic Acid (D)
The last two bases are AG
This is the consensus splice acceptor site.




Scroll through the gene and note how the intronic sequences are comprised largely of dispersed repeat sequences.
crumbs: 4  4: Interpret gene structure using *TERF1*

title: 4: Interpret gene structure using TERF1
section: Examine the terminal exon and 3’ UTR
text:
Examine the terminal exon and 3’ UTR
Navigate to the terminal TERF1 exon and zoom in:







TipTest your understanding




Which is the correct reading frame for this exon in your view?
What is the sequence of the stop codon?









TipAnswer






It will depend on your IGV instance but in this image it is the bottom frame as the stop codon coincides with the end of the terminal exon.
TGA




Zoom out to see the whole of the final exon.







TipTest your understanding




What is the approximate length of the 3’ UTR for TERF1?









TipAnswer





The UTR spans 73,960,358 to 73,958,372 so is 1,986 bases (approx. 2000 bp)
crumbs: 4  4: Interpret gene structure using *TERF1*

title: 5: Genes on the reverse strand: DMPK
text:
Let’s look at the DMPK gene. This gene is different from TERF1 as it is transcribed from the bottom strand relative to the chromosomal reference (the top strand). Exon 1 is on the right, and the terminal exon on the left. You can quickly navigate to DMPK (or any gene) by typing its name into the search bar.

Zoom in on one of the DMPK coding exons. To see the correct amino acid sequence for this gene, we will have to set the ‘reverse’ option so that IGV translates from the bottom strand - remember that it will still be running right to left.






Warning



Don’t forget to turn this option off again if you look at a gene or variants on the reference (top) strand.



Zoom out a bit more to get an overview of the other genes in the vicinity of DMPK. Some genes are in the same orientation as DMPK and transcribed from the bottom strand (e.g. SIX5, DMWD, RSPH6A) but others are transcribed from the top strand (e.g. BHMG1).
You should also see that many genes have a CpG island spanning exon 1. These regions are often (but not always) associated with the presence of H3K4me3 in ChIPseq data, indicating open chromatin.
crumbs: 5  5: Genes on the reverse strand: *DMPK*

title: 6: Load Platinum Genomes sequencing data
text:
Next, we will load some actual sequence data from the platinum genomes collection of tracks:

Shift-click samples NA12889, NA12890 and NA12877 and press OK.

The platinum genomes are derived from a reference genome dataset described in Eberle et al., 2017. In the study, the genomes of four grandparents, two parents and 11 children were sequenced on an Illumina HiSeq2000 to an average depth of 50× using 2×100 bp paired-end reads.
The ID of each sample is defined by adding the family identifier prefix (e.g. NA128) to each numbered individual (e.g. 77 would be NA12877). For this session, we will load in a mother-father-child trio (individuals 89, 90 and 77) from family NA128.

You may need to use the cog associated with each track to change the Track Height to get everything visible on your screen. You can also drag the tracks into an easier order using the handles at the side of each track.

We can speed up the display by removing tracks we no longer need (e.g. CpG, repeats and H3K4me3) by clicking their specific cog on the track and selecting remove.







Warning



Note that sometimes IGV still slows down when you load the sequence data and you may need to refresh the page if it gets stuck. Unfortunately, you will then need to change the genome to hg19 again and reload the relevant tracks again.
crumbs: 6  6: Load Platinum Genomes sequencing data

title: 7: Inspect reads and identify variants in MYO6
text:
Let’s zoom in and have a look at a region in the MYO6 gene of the trio in detail by typing the chromosome coordinates into the search box: chr6:76,525,195-76,525,5426.
MYO6 mutations are linked to autosomal dominant and autosomal recessive inherited hearing loss.






Warning



We will be examining variants in the top reference strand, so it is best to turn off the ‘reverse’ option for this region unless looking at whether a variant is synonymous



The mountain plot at the top of the display shows the read depth across the region (the scale here goes from 0 to 52x). Individual 100 bp reads are shown as grey rectangles - the arrow on the end indicating the direction of the read (you can use the scroll bar here to see more of the reads).

Where a base in a read is the same as the reference, it is coloured grey
Where a base in a read is different to the reference, it is coloured by base.


Zooming in even closer we can see the actual sequences and identify any differences between the reads and the reference.

To gauge whether any sequence differences might represent germline variants, we can examine the bases observed at each position by clicking on a base in the mountain plot at the top of each read track.







TipTest your understanding




What do you think is the germline genotype for NA12877 (the son) at position ch6:76,525,300?
What are the possible sources of the G read observed?









TipAnswer






This position appears to be homozygous A (A/A) because all the reads are the same
Most likely a sequencing error, but could possibly be a rare somatic variant




Moving along slightly to position 76,525,311:







TipTest your understanding




What is the reference sequence at position chr6:76,525,311?
What is the germline genotype at position chr6:76,525,311 for NA12877 (the son)?
How sure are we that this is not a sequencing error?









TipAnswer






The reference sequence at position chr6:76,525,311 is C
The germline genotype at position chr6:76,525,311 for NA12877 is Homozygous T (T/T)
All of the reads (51/51) were T at this position, unless this was a highly reproducible sequencing error, then there is a very low probability that the germline genotype is C/C and all the reads are error





Examine the reads for the other members of the trio.







TipTest your understanding




What are the genotypes at position chr6:76,525,311 for NA12889 and NA12890?
Are the predicted genotypes consistent with Mendelian expectations?









TipAnswer






Both parents are heterozygous T/C
The pattern does fit with Mendelian expectations: father T/C, mother T/C and son T/T suggest the son inherited a T from each parent




By clicking on the feature in the Common SNPs track we can see that this is a known SNP and gain additional information:







TipTest your understanding




What is the identifier (name) of the SNP at this position?
What is the minor allele frequency (MAF)?









TipAnswer






The SNP identifier is rs72890637
The MAF is 0.023
crumbs: 7  7: Inspect reads and identify variants in *MYO6*

title: 8: Investigate variants using Ensembl
text:
We can find out even more about this SNP using the Ensembl database. Enter the SNP identifier (rs72890637) into the Ensembl search box (If Ensembl search is down, use the direct link to the SNP)

Then click on the link in the Ensembl Feature explorer search results.

There are then links to various pieces of data about the SNP. Click on the Allele Frequency link.







TipTest your understanding




What is the minor allele frequency in Finland? (you may have to expand the gnomAD genomes v4.1 dataset)
How does that compare to the wider, non-Finnish European population?









TipAnswer






The MAF for Finnish Europeans is 9%
The wider European population MAF is 6%. Finland often differs from other European populations because of a phenomenon called the Finnish founder effect that has emerged because of a small founder population, various bottlenecks, geographic isolation and low immigration.
crumbs: 8  8: Investigate variants using Ensembl

title: 9: Genotypes, inheritance and haplotypes
text:
Let’s look at a few more variants. To start with, we’ll focus on rs1280055. We can jump straight to this SNP by typing its ID into the IGV search bar.







TipTest your understanding




What are the genotypes at rs1280055 for NA12877, NA12889 and NA12890?
Are they consistent with Mendelian inheritance patterns?









TipAnswer






The genotypes are C/C for NA12877 (child), G/C for NA12889 (father) and G/C for NA12890 (mother)
These are consistent with Mendelian inheritance and the child has inherited a C allele from each heterozygous parent




Scroll along a few hundred bases to the right and you should find another SNP - rs1280056.







TipTest your understanding




What are the genotypes at rs1280056 for NA12877, NA12889 and NA12890?









TipAnswer





The genotypes are A/A for NA12877 (child), A/G for NA12889 (father) and A/G for NA12890 (mother)



To determine which variants have been inherited together on the same chromosome, and hence which parents they likely came from, we can ‘phase’ the sequence to determine haplotypes. In the example below, a G at rs1280055 is always found with a G in rs1280056 in mate pairs that cover both SNPs. Conversely, a C in rs1280055 is always found with an A in rs1280056. This allows us to infer the haplotype for the sample.

By using paired reads, we can look at much longer sequence distances than the 100 bp length of each individual read.







Tip



To help, we can use “view as pairs” in the parents to look for direct physical evidence of the parental haplotypes. This setting adds a line between read-pairs in the sequencing data, allowing us to see sequence that comes from the same fragment and originated from a single physical position in the genome.

title: 10: Variant effect predictor with APOE
text:
Next, we’ll look at the APOE gene. You can quickly locate it using the search box.

Focus on the two common SNPs found in exon 4.

Start with the variant at position chr19:45,411,941 (rs429358).







TipTest your understanding




What is the nature of the polymorphism at the DNA level?
Does this variant change the amino acid sequence? (You will have to turn on translation and work out which is the reading frame by looking at exon 1)?
If so, from what to what?
What are the genotypes at this SNP for NA12877, NA12889 and NA12890?
What is the minor (alt) allele and the MAF?
What type of variant is this – would it impact the protein?









TipAnswer






The polymorphism at this site is C/T
Yes, this is a nonsynonymous mutation
The codon and amino acid changes from TGC (Cys) to CGC (Arg)
The genotypes are C/T for NA12877 (child), T/T for NA12889 (father) and C/T for NA12890 (mother)
The MAF for the minor (alt) C-allele is 18%
This missense variant is protein altering. It is associated with predisposition to late onset Alzheimer’s disease (amongst other associations)




We can use the variant effect predictor (VEP) tool to gain some insight into potential functional effects of a given variant. Navigate to the VEP site: https://www.ensembl.org/tools/vep






Warning



We will be using hg19/GRCh37 coordinates, so make sure you have the right genome version selected.



A VEP search string has to be in a set format:
19 45411941 45411941 T C

The first number is the Chromosome
The second number is the start position
The third number is the end position (for a SNP, this is the same as the start position)
The fourth character is the wild-type base
The fifth character is the variant base(s) that the position will change to

Press “Add” when you’ve entered the details of the variant. Set the submission name to something you will remember.

We can also add some additional analyses to the job by scrolling down to Job Options. For now, enable REVEL and CADD under Variant impact predictions. These will help us predict any effect that the variants might have.






Tip



REVEL (Rare Exome Variant Ensemble Learner) is a computational tool that predicts whether a missense variant is likely to be disease-causing by combining the results of multiple variant effect prediction algorithms into a single score between 0 and 1. Higher REVEL scores indicate a greater likelihood that the variant is pathogenic, while lower scores suggest it is more likely to be benign. Although there are no set thresholds, a general rule of thumb is:

0.8+ : Pathogenic
0.5-0.8 : Likely Pathogenic
0.2-0.5 : Likely benign
<0.2 : Benign

(Ioannidis NM, Rothstein JH, Pejaver V, et al. (2016) “REVEL: An Ensemble Method for Predicting the Pathogenicity of Rare Missense Variants.” American Journal of Human Genetics 99(4):877-885. DOI:10.1016/j.ajhg.2016.08.016)
CADD (Combined Annotation Dependent Depletion) is a variant prioritisation score that integrates multiple genomic annotations to predict the deleteriousness of genetic variants. Higher CADD PHRED scores indicate a greater likelihood of functional impact, with scores above 20 typically considered potentially damaging.
CADD scores are ranked so that a score of 10 places a variant among the top 10% most deleterious variants in the genome, while a score of 20 places it among the top 1%.
Although there are no set thresholds for CADD, a general rule of thumb is:

30+ : Deleterious
20-30 : Potentially deleterious
10-20 : Unlikely to be deleterious
<10 : Not deleterious

(Rentzsch P, Witten D, Cooper GM, Shendure J, Kircher M. (2019) “CADD: predicting the deleteriousness of variants throughout the human genome.” Nucleic Acids Research 47(D1):D886-D894. DOI:10.1093/nar/gky1016)





Screenshot from the original tutorial (slide 56).


Press “Run” when you’re ready. Your job will take a few minutes. Press Results when it has finished.







TipTest your understanding




What type of variant is this?
What might the REVEL score indicate about this variant? (You might have to click show annotations to see these details)
What might the CADD score indicate about this variant? (You might have to click show annotations to see these details)









TipAnswer






This is a missense variant
A REVEL score of 0.229 is low and would generally be interpreted as evidence that the variant is likely benign (not disease-causing).
A CADD PHRED score of 13.75 suggests the variant is unlikely to be deleterious. These low scores are probably because the MAF is high (~15%) and isn’t likely to be associated with anything too serious - remembering that Alzheimer disease is very common and very serious but usually only affects people after their reproductive age




There is another SNP a bit further downstream (rs7412) we will examine next.







TipTest your understanding




What is the nature of the polymorphism at the DNA level?
Does this variant change the amino acid sequence?
If so, from what to what?
What are the genotypes at this SNP for NA12877, NA12889 and NA12890?
Is this variant likely to be pathogenic? (check using VEP)









TipAnswer






The polymorphism is C/T
Yes, this is a non-synonymous mutation
The codon and amino acid changes from CGC (Arg) to (TGC) Cys
The variant has a higher REVEL score of 0.588 (use 19   45412079 45412079 C T to search)

title: Case Study: Alzheimer’s disease
text:
Genetic, environmental and lifestyle factors contribute to late onset Alzheimer’s disease (late-onset AD, LOAD), with genetic factors contributing approximately 60%. Variation at the APOE gene locus plays a contributory genetic role. APOE encodes a very low-density lipoprotein that helps remove cholesterol from the bloodstream. The exact functional role of the protein encoded by APOE in LOAD remains unclear.
The major APOE risk for LOAD is generally assumed to derive from the e2/e3/e4 haplotype system, with the e4 allele increasing risk for the disorder and the e2 allele being protective. The e2/e3/e4 haplotype system is defined by the two non-synonymous SNPs in APOE exon 4 that we just examined. One is a C/T SNP (rs429358) that encodes either cysteine (C) or arginine (R) at amino acid 130. The second site defining this haplotype system is a C/T SNP (rs7412), which again encodes arginine (R) or cysteine (C) at amino acid 176
The allelic compositions of the commonly investigated rs429358/rs7412 haplotypes are:
T–T for ε2
T–C for ε3
C–C for ε4

TipTest your understanding




What are the APOE exon 4 haplotypes for NA12877, NA12889 and NA12890 and their relative LOAD risk status?
Why might the C–T haplotype not be observed?









TipAnswer





The haplotypes and relative LOAD risk are:

NA12877: T–T APOE ε2 possibly protective, T–C APOE ε3 neutral
NA12889: T–T APOE ε2 possibly protective, T–T APOE ε2 possibly protective
NA12890: T–T APOE ε2 possibly protective, T–C APOE ε3 neutral

The C-T haplotype may not be observed, as the two variants are very close and the probability of a recombination event generating the fourth recombinant haplotype is very low

title: Case Study: Zellweger syndrome
text:
A family is referred to clinical genetics with a severely ill newborn child who has received a clinical diagnosis of probable Zellweger syndrome. This is an autosomal recessive systemic disorder characterised clinically by severe neurologic dysfunction, craniofacial abnormalities, and liver dysfunction, and biochemically by the absence of peroxisomes. Zellweger syndrome is characterised by locus heterogeneity and can be caused by mutations in any one of several genes, encoding proteins known as pexins, which are involved in peroxisome biogenesis. In order to try and provide a genetic diagnosis, whole exome sequencing was performed in the family and variants in a known Zellweger gene, PEX3, detected:

The data strongly support a diagnosis of Zellweger syndrome in the affected child, who is compound heterozygous for two predicted high-impact PEX3 variants, one frameshift and one premature stop variant, neither of which has been observed in gnomAD. Although the impact of the 143784092 variant is predicted as moderate, this allele is relatively frequent (~2% and 17% in Latinos), and at least 600 homozygotes have been observed, so it is unlikely to be a disease allele. The 143800237 variant is novel, but synonymous, so it is again unlikely pathogenic. Thus, each parent carries a different candidate pathogenic allele. The recurrence risk is 25% for each pregnancy, assuming the variants are confirmed to be in trans and causative.
